$L_1$, because it connects two points on the curve.
options.why: Identifies the secant chord rather than the tangent line.

options.text: Both lines have the same gradient and represent instantaneous rate.
options.why: Secant and tangent lines have distinct gradients for non-linear curves.

options.text: Neither line, as instantaneous rates cannot be represented by straight lines.
options.why: A tangent line geometrically defines the instantaneous rate.

questions.solution_text: $\text{The instantaneous rate of change at } x = 3\text{ is represented by the gradient of the tangent line, line } L_2.$

Point $P$
options.why: At point P the curve is rising, so the derivative is positive ($f'(x) > 0$).

options.text: Point $Q$
options.why: At the peak point Q the tangent is horizontal, so $f'(x) = 0$.

options.why: P and R have opposite derivative signs (positive at P, negative at R).

questions.solution_text: $\text{At point } R\text{, the curve slopes downward to the right, meaning the tangent gradient is negative } (f'(x) < 0).$

questions.question_text:
The table shows the gradient of secant lines between $x = 3$ and $x = 3+h$ for $f(x) = x^2$:
$\begin{array}{c|ccc} h & 0.1 & 0.01 & 0.001 \\ \hline m_{\text{secant}} & 6.1 & 6.01 & 6.001 \end{array}$
What is the estimated instantaneous rate of change $f'(3)$?

options.why: Takes the value for $h=0.1$ rather than finding the limiting value as $h \to 0$.
Evaluates $f(3) = 3^2 = 9$ rather than the gradient of the tangent.
Confuses the parameter $h \to 0$ with the value of the gradient.

questions.solution_text:
$\text{As } h \to 0\text{, the secant gradient values } 6.1, 6.01, 6.001\text{ approach } 6.$
$\text{Instantaneous rate } f'(3) = 6$

questions.question_text:
A roadside speed camera records a car travelling at $88\text{ km/h}$ as it passes the sensor.
Which rate of change does this reading represent?

options.text: Instantaneous speed, because it measures the speed at that exact point in time.
Average speed, because speed always involves an interval of distance and time.
options.why: Point sensors measure instantaneous speed at a single moment.

options.text: Average acceleration, because the car's speed is changing.
options.why: The reading is a speed measurement (km/h), not an acceleration.

options.text: Total distance, because it measures the length of the road.
options.why: The measurement is a rate of change with units km/h, not a distance.

questions.solution_text: $\text{The speed camera measures the speed at a single specific instant, which is the instantaneous speed.}$

questions.question_text: Which statement correctly defines the relationship between the derivative $f'(a)$ and the graph of $y = f(x)$?

options.text: $f'(a)$ is the gradient of the tangent line to the curve at $x = a$.
$f'(a)$ is the $y$-value of the curve at $x = a$.
options.why: Confuses the derivative $f'(a)$ with the function value $f(a)$.

options.text: $f'(a)$ is the gradient of the secant line between $x = 0$ and $x = a$.
options.why: Confuses the instantaneous tangent gradient with a secant from the origin.

options.text: $f'(a)$ is the area under the curve between $x = 0$ and $x = a$.
options.why: Confuses differentiation with integration.

questions.solution_text: $\text{By definition, the derivative } f'(a)\text{ is the gradient of the tangent line to } y = f(x)\text{ at } x = a.$

questions.question_text:
The vertex of the parabola $y = -(x - 4)^2 + 9$ is located at $(4, 9)$.
What is the value of the derivative $f'(4)$?

options.why: States the maximum $y$-value instead of the tangent gradient at the vertex.
States the $x$-coordinate of the vertex instead of the gradient.
States the leading coefficient of the quadratic instead of the tangent slope.

questions.solution_text:
$\text{At the vertex of a smooth parabola, the tangent line is horizontal.}$
$\text{A horizontal line has gradient } 0\text{, so } f'(4) = 0.$

questions.question_text: How can the approximation of the instantaneous rate of change at $x = 2$ using the average rate over $[2, 2+h]$ be improved?

options.text: By making the interval width $h$ smaller and closer to $0$.
By making the interval width $h$ larger.
options.why: Larger intervals deviate further from the local tangent slope.

options.text: By averaging the function values $f(2)$ and $f(2+h)$.
options.why: Averaging function values gives midpoint height, not slope.

options.text: By changing the base point from $x = 2$ to $x = 0$.
options.why: Changing the base point evaluates the rate at a different location.

questions.solution_text: $\text{The secant line rotates closer to the tangent line as the interval width } h\text{ approaches } 0.$

questions.question_text:
The graph of a temperature function $T(t)$ has a tangent at $t = 5$ with gradient $-3.5^{\circ}\text{C/min}$.
What does this value indicate about the temperature at $t = 5\text{ minutes}$?

options.text: The temperature is decreasing at an instantaneous rate of $3.5^{\circ}\text{C}$ per minute.
The temperature decreased by a total of $3.5^{\circ}\text{C}$ in the first $5\text{ minutes}$.
options.why: Confuses total temperature change with the instantaneous rate.

options.text: The temperature is increasing by $3.5^{\circ}\text{C}$ every minute.
options.why: Ignores the negative sign, which indicates cooling/decreasing temperature.

options.text: The temperature at $t = 5$ is $-3.5^{\circ}\text{C}$.
options.why: Confuses the rate of change $T'(5)$ with the temperature $T(5)$.

questions.solution_text: $\text{A derivative value of } T'(5) = -3.5^{\circ}\text{C/min}\text{ means the temperature is decreasing at an instantaneous rate of } 3.5^{\circ}\text{C/min}\text{ at } t = 5\text{ minutes}.$
